results.name: Railroad_Stations
results.title: Light Rail Stations
results.description:
This polyline feature contains geographic and attribute information for the purpose of depicting railroad stations within the City of SeaTac and surrounding communities. The data was obtained from Sound Transit Office of Policy and Planning: GIS Services and modified to meet City needs. The data was originally created by Sound Transit to support Sound Transit's Link light rail line of business function including planning, engineering design, siting, identification and assessment of impacted parcels, environmental assessment, and general mapping. Supports map display and query (in ST Map Explorer) and general mapping agency-wide.


The data presented in this dataset in some cases represent planned sections of rail stations and is subject to change without notice.

Incorporated in February 1990, the City of SeaTac is located in the Pacific Northwest, approximately midway between the cities of Seattle and Tacoma in the State of Washington. SeaTac is a vibrant community, economically strong, environmentally sensitive, and people-oriented. The City boundaries surround the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, (approximately 3 square miles in area) which is owned and operated by the Port of Seattle. 

For additional information regarding the City of SeaTac, its people, or services, please visit https://www.seatacwa.gov. For additional information regarding City GIS data or maps, please visit https://www.seatacwa.gov/our-city/maps-and-gis.

results.name: Metro_Transit_System_Operational_Layers_2024_Fall
results.title: Metro Transit System Operational Layers 2024 Fall
results.description:
Operational layers for the Metro Transit System web map. The layers are 
park & rides and clickable route label areas.

Park & ride locations are taken from the Adobe Illustrator master 
system map. Those location points have been joined to the KCGIS 
enterprise park & ride layer to derive the number of parking spaces.
 Park & ride names have been coordinated to be consistent with the 
enterprise data layer and the Illustrator map labels, with defference to
 the later when there are conflicting details.

The route label areas have been organized into a set of layers by 
definition queries on agency and service categories. The service 
categories are derived from available agency website schedule and map 
page links so that URLs can be formulated to take users to pages that 
represent specific categories of service, for example weekday, weekday, 
Saturday, holiday, etc.

results.title: Lightrail stations
results.description:
As Seattle continues to grow, there will be opportunities for continued expansion of the regional Link light rail system. Potential expansion corridors are based on STP analysis as well as a review of previous Sound Transit and regional plans. These concepts reflect Seattle’s interest in continued growth of the rail system and would require additional analysis and evaluation. No funding is identified for these conceptual expansion corridors; the committed ST3 program extends into the 2040s.

Regional growth and changing employment patterns are likely to increase demand for all-day service and improved off-peak direction travel on Sounder, the Puget Sound region’s commuter rail service operated by Sound Transit. Future investments, such as midday service, higher frequencies all day, and electrification could be important investments to making Sounder a key part of the region’s high-capacity rail network. Additional stations located in key growth centers should be considered to improve access and network connectivity
results.snippet: Both existing and future light rail station locations within Seattle

results.title: Buses from Here
results.description:
This story map was prepared to accompany a presentation by Patrick Jankanish at the October 6, 2021, King County GIS User Group meeting. It describes some of the design and production considerations and techniques for a set of four spider-wayfinding maps and graphics for Sound Transit Link light rail stations.

On October 2, 2021, Sound Transit opened three new Link stations on the 1 Line in north Seattle: Northgate, Roosevelt, and U District. The new maps were created for these stations and the previously opened University of Washington Station.

The maps were conceived and developed into a proof of concept by Derek Holmer of King County Metro Transit. Derek led the effort to produce the set of finished maps. The King County GIS Center's Spatial Services team consulted on the design and executed the production of the maps.
results.snippet: Creating spider maps for Sound Transit’s Link light rail stations

results.title: Metro Transit System: March 2020 - With Medical Facilities
results.description:
This is a copy of the Metro Transit System map which is available in the Metro Transit System map viewer app. The locations of hospital and other medical facilities location have been added to this copy for display in a new version of the system viewer app.

This web map displays the artwork from the Adobe-Illustrator-based master Metro Transit System map. The artwork is presented here as a set of rasterized, tiled map layers. The purpose of the map is simple navigation of the static artwork, plus the ability for users to print selected map extents in a print-enabled map viewer app.

Map users can also click or tap park & ride symbols on the map to display more information, and click or tap bus route labels to display links to online schedules and route maps.

Service information on this map is effective March 20, 2020 through September 18, 2020.

The map was produced by the King County GIS Center and King County Metro Transit. For information about the cartography, please contact Patrick Jankanish.

results.title: Countywide Center
results.description:
Countywide growth centers (CWC) are intended to serve important roles as places for equitably concentrating jobs, housing, shopping, and recreational opportunities


Often smaller downtowns, high-capacity transit station areas, or neighborhood centers that are linked by transit, provide a mix of housing and services, and serve as focal points for local and county investment. In August 2021, the City of Federal Way applied for and was successfully designated a Countywide Center (CWC) Candidate by the Growth Management Planning Council.


The CWC designation requires the city to prepare a subarea plan that will be adopted as part of the 2024 Periodic Update to the Comprehensive Plan. The subarea plan is currently referred to as South Station Subarea Plan. Visit  https://engagefw.com/southstation for more information.

results.title: Seattle Transit to Beaches & Parks Map, Nayzet Pena, Fall 2023
results.description:
The Seattle Transit to Beaches & Parks Map features a collection of data that visually represents the public Seattle transit in relation to the swimming beaches and parks in the area. The map features lines and stations for Sound Transit public data including Link Light Rail, Sounder, and Express services. It also has Seattle swimming beaches and park data. In particular the map shows parks within 550 feet of any transit stop, and swimming beaches a mile from any transit stop. Each of these features have individual and unique symbols to represent them, along with details available in the pop-ups that appear. 

To use this map use your mouse to click and explore the different features. By clicking on a line, point, or shape a pop up will appear with additional information on the item. You will note that to keep the map less cluttered some features only appear if you are scrolled in close enough. 

The sources for the different layers are listed below:
- Sound Transit Public Data obtained from Sound Transit Open Transit Data (Added from downloaded file)
- Swimming Beaches data obtained from Seattle GeoData website (Added from web) 
- Park data obtained from Seattle GeoData website (Added from web)
- Swimming Beaches a Mile from Transit Stop data obtained from Seattle GeoData website and Sound Transit Open Transit Data  (Analysis Tools)
- Parks 550 ft from Transit data obtained from Seattle GeoData website and Sound Transit Open Transit Data  (Analysis Tools)
results.snippet: This map shows the public Seattle transit, as well as swimming beaches and parks in the area.

results.title: Tacoma Link Phase 2 Alignment, In Red (Begins West of Tacoma Dome Station)
results.description:
This proposal details alternative Link Light Rail alignments for direct rail service to Central Tacoma, the Central Tacoma Link Extension (CTLE). This proposal should be contrasted with the current Sound Transit effort to terminate the multi-billion dollar rail line at Tacoma Dome Station—a park-n-ride facility tailored to the suburbs.

Alignment options are broken into three groups with two options each, and can be reviewed individually within the "Layers" tab.

A terminal group with three options: a Commerce Street option under 923 Commerce Street, a Pacific Avenue option under the street, or a visionary extension to the Hilltop jobs core (an alternative to the Sound Transit "programmed" Tacoma Mall extension).

A city approach group with two options: a west approach along Pacific Avenue, or an east approach along I-705.

A river crossing group with two options: a north approach with a clear span bridge, or a south approach closer to I-5.
results.snippet:
Review of alternative alignments for a Central Tacoma Link Extension (CTLE), which would deliver Sound Transit Link trains into the heart of Tacoma. 

The preferred option is the promised conversion of the existing Tacoma Light Rail starter line.

results.name: SubareaPlanPaineFieldBoeingEvtMIC
results.title: SubareaPlanPaineFieldBoeingEvtMIC
results.description:
https://www.psrc.org/media/10451

Jurisdiction Comments / Additional Context:
The City of Everett and Snohomish County are committed to working together to complete a Subarea Plan for the Paine Field/Boeing Everett Manufacturing Industrial Center by December 31, 2027. Both jurisdictions recognize the regional significance of the Paine Field/Boeing Everett MIC as a center for economic activities and employment. The previous Subarea Plan was repealed when the City of Everett adopted its new Comprehensive Plan on June 18, 2025. The City of Everett and Snohomish County are in the process of developing a new Subarea Plan. The Subarea Plan will assist both jurisdictions in meeting emerging economic trends, land use demands, and planning for future infrastructure investments. In 2019, the Paine Field commercial air terminal opened for passenger service. Paine Field has the newest commercial airport terminal in Washington State, with commercial air routes servicing nearly a dozen destinations in the western United States. As part of Sound Transit’s Everett Link Extension, light rail will connect from Lynnwood City Center to Downtown Everett. Sound Transit is planning for the SW Everett Industrial Center station within the Paine Field/Boeing Everett MIC. The Sound Transit Board will tentatively make a final decision on the station location in late 2027.
results.snippet: Matthew Siddons, Senior Planner with the Snohomish County Planning and Development Services, states that "The Puget Sound Regional Council (PSRC) is currently undertaking Regional Center Redesignations. As part of this process, PSRC has requested that a new Subarea Plan be developed for the Paine Field Boeing Everett Manufacturing Industrial Center (MIC), which includes areas within both the City of Everett and Snohomish County."

results.title: ORCA fare outlets
results.description:
ORCA fare outlets.  This includes Ticket Vending Machines (TVM), customer service centers and retail fare outlets.  This list is updated by Sound Transit as needed.

Attribute definitions:
Name – Retail business, Station name or Customer Service Center Name
Location – Street address
City - City
Zip – Zip Code
OutletType – Outlet description, (Retailer With Cards, TVM (Ticket Vending Machine), ORCA Customer Service Office)
County – County location (Example: King)
FacNum – Internal use.
Notes -  General note regarding the location (Example: Inside Safeway)
Lat – Latitude of facility (Example: 47.62)
Lon – Longitude of facility (Example: -122.30)
ListCity - The city, as per the officially published ORCA fare outlet list (Example: ‘Southeast Seattle’ or ‘Bellevue’
RailType – Rail tickets available: Example: ‘N/A’ [No rail tickets available] or ‘Link’)

results.title: Olympia Express Service Restoration
results.description:
Option 1 is the restoration of service as it was pre-COVID. This service option would see the return of Route 612, as well as service to Tacoma Dome Station. The 620 would revert to its previous alignment, operating only on the weekend and terminating at the Tacoma Mall.

Serving Tacoma Dome Station on weekdays allows for good connections with both Pierce Transit and Sound Transit Services, with Sound Transit redundancy at the 512 Park & Ride.  Service to Tacoma Dome does have substantial impacts on reliability requiring additional time to be included in the service, limiting the number of trips that can be provided each day. Reliability is further diminished by the redundancy of the 512 Park and Ride stop.  

This option would be the most familiar for historical riders, and likely the easiest to implement. Connections are available to Sound and Pierce Transit from Lakewood Station, Tacoma Dome Station, and Tacoma Mall Transit Center.
results.snippet: October 2023

results.title: Transit Infrastructure
results.description:
While the City doesn't run the buses or light rail trains, we do work closely with King County Metro, Sound Transit, and other transit providers on major service and infrastructure changes within the city limits. We enhance transit through:

Transit Service. The Seattle Transit Measure (Proposition 1) provides funding for the City to purchase transit service from King County Metro. We also contribute funding for transit service on both streetcars with sponsorship funds, fare-box revenue, and other funding sources. 

Planning and Policy. We updated the Transit Master Plan in 2016 and regularly coordinate with Metro, Sound Transit, and other City departments on transit improvement projects and station area planning.

Seattle Streetcar. We own the South Lake Union and First Hill streetcar lines.  We contract with Metro for operations. Work on a streetcar line to connect the two existing lines is underway, read more about the Center City Connector project.

Corridor Improvements. Levy to Move Seattle (a voter-approved levy) provides funding for transit corridor improvements, including seven new RapidRide corridors. We plan and build street, signal, bus stop facility, and technology improvements that increase bus speeds and enhance passenger comfort along key corridors. View current capital projects.

results.title: Central Tacoma Link Extension (CTLE) 2021
results.description:
This proposal details a superior Link Light Rail alignment for direct rail service to Central Tacoma, the Central Tacoma Link Extension (CTLE). This proposal should be contrasted with the current Sound Transit effort to terminate the multi-billion dollar rail line at Tacoma Dome Station—a transit facility tailored to the suburbs—via a route requiring overly complex engineering and civil structures. The trackways of the CTLE take advantage of existing rail rights-of-way and wide roadways, and will feature strict separation from vehicular traffic. The modern prototype of the surface sections of the extension can already be found on Pacific Avenue itself.

Differing voltages between the existing streetcar line and Link Light Rail present a problem across the shared trackage through Union Station, but are resolved by dual-traction technologies. Dual-traction trams or voltage conversion systems are commonly utilized by tram networks throughout the world.

This proposal echoes a system first constructed in 1902 for the Puget Sound Electric Railway, albeit with modal separation that will ensure timely and effective services through Pacific Avenue and the urban core of Tacoma. 

This proposal was designed using Sound Transit design criteria for light rail infrastructure and facilities.

Note: The Central Tacoma Link Extension (CTLE) is designed to integrate fully with Union and Tacoma Dome Stations, providing seamless transfers to the city's streetcar, bus rapid-transit and core bus network, the SPIRE Regional Rail System, and the Central Washington High-Speed Rail Line.
results.snippet: A complete overview of the Link Light Rail extension proposal for rail services into Central Tacoma (in red).

results.title: Discovering Seattle: Transit, Beaches, & Parks
results.description:
Seattle is a city located in the Pacific Northwest of the United States. With features reminiscent of the geography, the city grants the opportunity to explore nature through their transit. Notably, the Seattle public transit is one of the best in the country. As such, using it to access fun recreational activities can be expected when visiting.

The ability of Seattle's transit, Sound Transit, to access parks and swimming beaches will be explored as we continue.

This map aims to conduct that analysis. Data was collected from Sound Transit as well as open data resources for the city of Seattle. These are represented by the transit lines, swimming beaches, and parks on the map. The symbols representing each are seen in the legend to the right.

results.title: King County Metro System in Seattle
results.description:
Industry History

King County Metro Transit is King County’s first county-wide transit system. In 2018, the American Public Transportation Association awarded King County Metro for the Outstanding Public Transportation System Achievement Award. It was recognized as one of the best, large transit agencies in North America and operates Central Link Light Rail, Seattle Streetcar lines, RapidRide buses, amongst many other services.

Since its creation in 1973, Metro has applied for and received a federal Urban Mass Transit Administration grant of $86.3 million. Through this grant, the agency has built suburban transit centers and park-and-ride lots. It has also funded articulated, bending buses that would increase transport capacity. In the 1980s, they embarked on a plan to create a downtown bus tunnel which began operation in 1990. In 1994, Metro Transit merged with King County in a partnership best illustrated by Metro’s 2000 agreement to transfer the Seattle Bus Tunnel to Sound Transit for use as its light-rail tunnel (Kershner). In 2009, Metro provided more than 110 million passenger trips and carried passengers 496 million miles on its fixed-route system (King County Metro Strategic Plan).
results.snippet: Examining the impact of public transportation

results.title: Is Parking at UW T really worse than in UW Seattle?
results.description:
The first week on campus always brings the same conversation that can be heard from Tioga to Joy; "There's not enough parking". Despite having free access to all South Sound transit options (it's included with your Husky Card) many students and faculty still prefer to drive a car and park them on campus until they need them again. A comparison is often made that The UW Seattle has better car infrastructure than UWT. A cursory glance at a map of the two campuses might challenge that notion but as the critique persists let's take a closer look.

One of the first things to consider when comparing campuses is the size difference. The University of Washington Seattle is comprised of 649 total buildings. Whereas the Tacoma campus currently has 23 buildings with a 24th under construction.
results.snippet: We look at a commonly raised complaint

results.title: CID Construction Approach and Duration Study Results
results.description:
In March 2023, the Sound Transit board adopted motion M2023-18, which identified a preferred alternative for the Ballard Link Extension project. As part of this motion, the board also directed staff to further study ways to minimize or eliminate construction impacts to the Chinatown-International District (CID) and to significantly reduce the duration and effects of construction. 

This website provides information on construction duration drivers and construction activities associated with the following CID Station Alternatives.

Additionally, this website provides an overview of the refinement ideas that emerged for the 4th Avenue Shallow Alternative to reduce construction duration and impacts.

To learn about all alternatives being studied for the Ballard Link Extension, please visit our Online Open House.

More information can also be found in the report on construction approach and duration for CID Station alternatives.
results.snippet: Information on construction duration drivers and construction activities associated with the following CID Station Alternatives.
